Intersection bodies represent a remarkable class of geometric objects associated with sections of star bodies and invoking   Radon transforms, generalized cosine transforms, and the relevant Fourier analysis. The main focus of this article is interrelation between generalized cosine transforms of different kinds in the context of their application to investigation of a certain family of intersection bodies, which we call $\lam$-intersection bodies. The latter include $k$-intersection bodies (in the sense of A. Koldobsky) and unit balls of finite-dimensional subspaces of $L_p$-spaces. In particular, we show that restrictions onto lower dimensional subspaces of the spherical Radon transforms and the generalized cosine transforms preserve their integral-geometric structure. We apply this result to the study of sections of $\lam$-intersection bodies. New characterizations of this class of bodies are obtained and examples are given. We also review some known facts and give them new proofs.

The main focus of this article is the interplay among various types of generalized cosine transforms and their application to the study of a particular family of intersection bodies, which we call $\lam$-intersection bodies. This family includes $k$-intersection bodies (in the sense of A. Koldobsky) and unit balls of finite-dimensional subspaces of $L_p$-spaces. In particular, we show that restricting spherical Radon transforms and generalized cosine transforms to lower-dimensional subspaces preserves their integral-geometric structure. We apply this result to the study of sections of $\lam$-intersection bodies, obtain new characterizations of this class of bodies, and provide examples. We also review several known results and present new proofs of them.

Intersection bodies are an important class of geometric objects closely connected with sections of star bodies, spherical Radon transforms, generalized cosine transforms, and methods from Fourier analysis. These connections make them a natural meeting point for ideas from convex geometry, integral geometry, and harmonic analysis.

The article investigates the relationships among several types of generalized cosine transforms and uses these relationships to study a broader family of objects known as \(\lambda\)-intersection bodies. This family encompasses several significant examples, including \(k\)-intersection bodies and the unit balls of finite-dimensional subspaces of \(L_p\)-spaces. Thus, the framework of \(\lambda\)-intersection bodies provides a unified way to examine geometric classes that have traditionally been studied separately.

A central result concerns the behavior of spherical Radon transforms and generalized cosine transforms when restricted to lower-dimensional subspaces. The authors show that these restrictions preserve the essential integral-geometric structure of the transforms. In other words, passing to a subspace does not destroy the fundamental relationships between sections, transforms, and the measures or functions that represent the bodies under consideration.

These results are then applied to the study of sections of \(\lambda\)-intersection bodies. The authors obtain new characterizations of such bodies, construct additional examples, and clarify how the class behaves under taking lower-dimensional sections. Their approach also yields new proofs of several previously known facts, demonstrating that the theory of generalized cosine transforms offers a coherent and effective framework for understanding intersection bodies and their extensions.

The article develops a unified analytic and integral-geometric framework for studying generalized cosine transforms, spherical Radon transforms, and their connections with Fourier analysis. Its principal objects are \(\lambda\)-intersection bodies, a class of star bodies that extends several notions central to the modern theory of convex and star-shaped bodies. Important special cases include Koldobsky’s \(k\)-intersection bodies and unit balls of finite-dimensional subspaces of \(L_p\)-spaces.

A central theme is the behavior of the relevant transforms under restriction to lower-dimensional linear subspaces. Although generalized cosine and spherical Radon transforms are naturally defined on spheres of a fixed dimension, the article shows that their essential integral-geometric structure is preserved when the underlying functions, distributions, or bodies are restricted to subspheres. The resulting restriction formulas connect transforms in the ambient space with corresponding transforms inside a subspace and clarify how their positivity and representation properties pass from one dimension to another.

These results are then applied to \(\lambda\)-intersection bodies. Using the Fourier-analytic description of homogeneous distributions associated with star bodies, the article obtains new criteria for determining when a body belongs to the class of \(\lambda\)-intersection bodies. The restriction theory also explains how this property behaves under taking sections and provides a systematic way to construct examples in lower dimensions from bodies in higher-dimensional spaces.

The general framework recovers Koldobsky’s theory of \(k\)-intersection bodies for appropriate integral values of the parameter. It also relates \(\lambda\)-intersection bodies to the geometry of finite-dimensional subspaces of \(L_p\). In particular, the Fourier and transform characterizations make it possible to identify relevant \(L_p\)-unit balls as members of suitable classes of generalized intersection bodies and to compare these classes across different parameter ranges.

Besides producing new characterizations and examples, the approach gives alternative proofs of several previously known results. By treating cosine transforms, Radon transforms, and Fourier transforms as different manifestations of the same underlying structure, the article simplifies dimension-reduction arguments and makes explicit the links between convex geometry, harmonic analysis, and integral geometry. Overall, it provides a flexible method for studying generalized intersection bodies and for transferring geometric information between ambient spaces and their lower-dimensional subspaces.

## Intersections, the Radon Transform, and Fourier Analysis

The geometry of intersections is closely connected with two fundamental tools of analysis: the Radon transform and the Fourier transform. Together, these methods translate geometric information about a set into analytic data that can be studied through integration and frequency analysis.

For a sufficiently regular function \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{C}\), the hyperplane Radon transform is defined by

\[
Rf(\theta,s)
=
\int_{\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:\,x\cdot\theta=s\}}
f(x)\,d\sigma(x),
\]

where \(\theta\in S^{n-1}\), \(s\in\mathbb{R}\), and \(d\sigma\) denotes surface measure on the hyperplane. Thus, \(Rf(\theta,s)\) records the integral of \(f\) over the hyperplane perpendicular to \(\theta\) at signed distance \(s\) from the origin.

If \(f\) is the indicator function of a body \(K\subset\mathbb{R}^n\), then

\[
R\mathbf{1}_K(\theta,s)
\]

measures the \((n-1)\)-dimensional volume of the intersection

\[
K\cap\{x:x\cdot\theta=s\}.
\]

Consequently, the Radon transform provides a natural analytic description of the sections of a geometric object.

Its relationship with the Fourier transform is expressed by the Fourier slice theorem. If \(\mathcal{F}_s\) denotes the one-dimensional Fourier transform in the variable \(s\), then

\[
\mathcal{F}_s\big(Rf(\theta,\cdot)\big)(\tau)
=
\widehat f(\tau\theta).
\]

In other words, the Fourier transform of the hyperplane data in a fixed direction equals the restriction of the \(n\)-dimensional Fourier transform of \(f\) to the line passing through the origin in that direction. This identity is the central bridge between intersection data and frequency-space information.

The connection has important consequences. If all hyperplane integrals of a function are known, then its Fourier transform can be recovered along every radial line. Under suitable assumptions, this determines the original function. The same principle forms the mathematical basis of computed tomography: measurements of line or plane integrals from many directions are inverted to reconstruct an unknown density.

In convex geometry, central intersections are especially significant. For a star-shaped body \(K\), the volume of the section perpendicular to \(\theta\),

\[
\operatorname{vol}_{n-1}(K\cap\theta^\perp),
\]

can be represented through a spherical Radon transform of a power of the radial function of \(K\). Fourier-analytic methods then allow one to compare sections, characterize intersection bodies, and investigate whether geometric inequalities for sections imply corresponding inequalities for total volume.

Thus, intersection geometry, the Radon transform, and Fourier analysis describe three aspects of the same structure. Intersections provide the geometric measurements, the Radon transform organizes those measurements, and the Fourier transform reveals how they encode—and can reconstruct—the underlying object.

counterfactuals.output: We study generalized cosine transforms on the sphere as a meromorphic family of rotation-equivariant operators and investigate their role in the theory of \(\lambda\)-intersection bodies. Using spherical harmonics and homogeneous distributions, we derive spectral formulas, identify exceptional parameters, and establish inversion and range characterizations. These results yield a unified analytic description of \(\lambda\)-intersection bodies in terms of positivity properties of generalized cosine transforms and Fourier transforms of homogeneous extensions of radial functions. We examine the dependence of the resulting classes on \(\lambda\), prove inclusion and approximation results, and recover classical intersection bodies as a distinguished special case. Applications include new criteria for recognizing \(\lambda\)-intersection bodies and connections with sections of star bodies, positive-definite distributions, and isometric embeddings of normed spaces into \(L_p\).

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize a paper studying intersection bodies, spherical Radon transforms, generalized cosine transforms, and sections of star bodies.
counterfactuals.output:
The paper develops an analytic framework for studying **intersection bodies and lower-dimensional sections of origin-symmetric star bodies**. Its main tools are the **spherical Radon transform** and a meromorphic family of **generalized cosine transforms**.

### Main ideas

- A star body is encoded by its radial function on the sphere.
- Volumes of central sections can be written as spherical Radon transforms of powers of that radial function.
- Classical and generalized intersection bodies are therefore characterized by whether certain radial-function powers lie in the range of a Radon transform—or, equivalently, are generalized cosine transforms of positive measures.
- The paper establishes inversion and factorization relations between these transforms, often using spherical harmonics and analytic continuation.
- These identities clarify when a candidate body can be realized from sections of another star body and expose positivity conditions that distinguish genuine intersection bodies from broader distributional classes.

### Significance

The work unifies geometric definitions of intersection bodies with harmonic-analytic ones. It converts questions about section volumes into range, inversion, and positivity problems for operators on the sphere. This provides:

- alternative characterizations of intersection-body classes;
- tools for constructing examples and counterexamples;
- extensions to sections of arbitrary codimension;
- a clearer connection between convex geometry, integral geometry, and harmonic analysis.

Overall, the paper shows that generalized cosine transforms provide a flexible common language for understanding spherical Radon transforms, intersection bodies, and the geometry of central sections.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a scholarly abstract explaining how restrictions of spherical Radon and generalized cosine transforms to lower-dimensional subspaces preserve their integral-geometric structure, with applications to $\lambda$-intersection bodies.
counterfactuals.output: We investigate the behavior of spherical Radon transforms and generalized cosine transforms under restriction to lower-dimensional linear subspaces. By identifying a subspace with its induced unit sphere and using the corresponding invariant measures, we show that restriction is governed by natural intertwining relations: ambient transforms descend to transforms of the same integral-geometric type, with parameters and homogeneity adjusted according to the codimension. Thus the associated kernels, incidence relations, and rotation-equivariance are preserved rather than replaced by ad hoc lower-dimensional constructions. These identities provide a unified mechanism for transferring analytic and geometric information between dimensions, including positivity, distributional representations, and range characterizations. As an application, we study sections of \(\lambda\)-intersection bodies. The transform characterization of this class implies that suitable central sections inherit a lower-dimensional \(\lambda\)-intersection-body structure, subject to the expected parameter shift and positivity conditions. The resulting framework clarifies the stability of intersection-body-type classes under sections and connects dimensional reduction in convex geometry with functorial properties of spherical integral transforms.

### Overview

\(\lambda\)-intersection bodies form a continuous, Fourier-analytic extension of the classical theory of intersection bodies. For an origin-symmetric star body \(K\subset\mathbb R^n\), membership is defined through the positivity or measure representation of the homogeneous distribution associated with \(\|x\|_K^{-\lambda}\), with analytic continuation used for negative parameters. At integer values \(\lambda=k\), the construction recovers Koldobsky’s \(k\)-intersection bodies; for \(\lambda=-p\), it also encompasses unit balls of finite-dimensional subspaces of \(L_p\).

The theory yields equivalent characterizations in terms of Fourier transforms of homogeneous distributions, generalized cosine and spherical Radon transforms, and positive measures on the sphere. These formulations connect geometric section data with embeddings of normed spaces into \(L_p\)-type spaces. Explicit examples—including \(\ell_q\)-balls, bodies of revolution, and smooth perturbations of the Euclidean ball—illustrate how the classes depend on \(\lambda\), distinguish them from classical intersection bodies, and show that the resulting hierarchy contains genuinely new geometric phenomena.
